name: secure-subprocess
description: Approach for invoking external processes safely. Treat all input as hostile. Never compose shell strings from interpolated values.

metadata.approach: Pass arguments as a list, never as a string. Avoid shell=True. Validate / allowlist any executable name that comes from configuration or user input. Set explicit cwd, env, and timeout.
checks: arguments are a list (not a single string)
shell=False (or omitted)
no string concatenation of untrusted input into the command
cwd is set explicitly when relative paths matter
timeout= is set for any command that could hang

name: money-decimal-precision
description: Approach for any code that handles currency, accounting, billing, or invoicing values.

metadata.approach: Use decimal.Decimal with explicit context (precision + ROUND_HALF_EVEN for finance). Never use float for money. Persist as integer minor units (cents, paise) or as string-decoded Decimal — never as JSON float.
checks: all monetary variables are decimal.Decimal (or integer minor units)
no arithmetic mixes Decimal with float
rounding mode is explicit (ROUND_HALF_EVEN for finance)
serialization preserves precision (string or integer, not float)
comparisons use Decimal-aware equality, not float tolerance
examples_good: from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_EVEN\namount = Decimal('19.99').quantize(Decimal('0.01'), rounding=ROUND_HALF_EVEN)

name: structured-concurrency-async
description: Approach for asyncio code that spawns multiple concurrent tasks.

metadata.approach: Use asyncio.TaskGroup (3.11+) for structured concurrency. Sibling cancellation is handled automatically. Always handle CancelledError by re-raising; never suppress it. Bound concurrency with a Semaphore when fan-out is unbounded.
checks: asyncio.TaskGroup is used (not asyncio.gather) for ≥2 concurrent tasks
CancelledError is re-raised, never silently swallowed
unbounded fan-out is gated by a Semaphore
no task is created without something awaiting its completion or cancellation
examples_good: async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:\n    tg.create_task(work(a))\n    tg.create_task(work(b))
examples_bad: asyncio.gather(*[work(x) for x in items])  # no concurrency cap, sibling-cancel semantics weak

name: crypto-secrets-not-random
description: Approach for any code generating tokens, session IDs, password salts, or anything an attacker could guess from output.

metadata.approach: Use the secrets module — never random. random is seeded predictably and is not cryptographically secure. For passwords use bcrypt/argon2id, never raw SHA-256.
checks: no use of random module for security values
secrets.token_urlsafe / secrets.token_hex / secrets.choice are used
passwords are hashed with bcrypt, argon2id, or scrypt — not raw SHA/MD5
constant-time comparison (hmac.compare_digest) for secret equality

name: user-input-untrusted-by-default
description: Approach for handling any value originating outside the trust boundary (HTTP request, file upload, env var, CLI arg, message queue).

metadata.approach: Validate at the boundary, not after the value has propagated. Reject malformed input loudly. Never trust length, type, encoding, or shape — assert each. Use Pydantic / dataclass validators where possible.
checks: validation happens at the boundary (handler / parser), not deep inside business logic
validation is structural (type + shape) AND semantic (allowed values)
max-size limits are enforced (string length, list length, dict depth)
encoding is asserted (utf-8 explicitly, not platform default)
rejection produces an error response with a stable schema
examples_good: class UserInput(BaseModel):\n    email: EmailStr\n    name: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=100)
examples_bad: if request.json: do_thing(request.json['name'])  # no validation, blind trust

name: sql-parameterized-queries
description: Approach for any database query that includes a value derived from user input or external data.

metadata.approach: Use parameterized queries (?, $1, :name) — never string-format SQL with values. Use the database driver's quoting; never write your own. ORMs (SQLAlchemy, Django) parameterize automatically; raw drivers require explicit parameter binding.
checks: all values from outside the trust boundary are passed as parameters, not formatted into the SQL string
table and column names are not user-controllable; if they must be, they're validated against an allowlist
LIKE patterns escape % and _ when matching user input literally
the ORM/driver handles quoting — no manual escape functions
examples_bad: cursor.execute(f'SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = {email!r}')  # injection-prone

name: error-handling-fail-loud
description: Approach for exception handling — when to catch, when to let it bubble.

metadata.approach: Catch only exceptions you can meaningfully respond to. Bare except: and except Exception: at framework boundaries are smells unless they re-raise after logging. Never silently swallow. Distinguish recoverable (retry, fallback) from unrecoverable (crash, alert).
checks: except clauses name specific exception types, not bare or Exception
exceptions that aren't handled are re-raised, not converted to None or default values
logging at the catch site includes the original exception (use logger.exception or chain via raise … from)
no `except X: pass` patterns unless the comment explicitly justifies why pass is correct

name: logging-structured-and-no-secrets
description: Approach for emitting log lines from production code.

metadata.approach: Use structured logging (extra= or a JSON formatter) so log fields are machine-queryable. Never log secrets, tokens, PII, or full request bodies. Set sensible defaults for sensitive field redaction.
checks: secrets, tokens, passwords, API keys are never logged (even in DEBUG)
PII (email, phone, address) is hashed or redacted before logging
log level is appropriate (DEBUG for development, INFO for events, WARNING for unusual, ERROR for failures)
exception traces use logger.exception, not str(e)
no use of print() in library / production code
